business-system-map.text: The offboarding ticket said the contractor was gone. Ninety days later an auditor finds her SSO account still active, still syncing to Salesforce, still on the approvals list — because six teams each owned one system and nobody owned the map between them.

An enterprise SaaS rollout is never one app — it is identity, roles, workflow, integration, audit, and governance wired together, each owned by a different team. The Business System Map is the smallest accurate picture of how those layers connect, so access correctness and audit evidence have somewhere to live before you configure anything.

business-system-map.prompt: You are asked to "map" a new SaaS system before rollout. Do you list every application the company runs — or something else? And what makes a map USEFUL rather than merely complete?
business-system-map.reveal: A logo inventory is complete and worthless — it hides the failure. The dangerous gaps live on the EDGES: SSO grants login, but SCIM provisioning decides what you can do; a deprovision event has to travel from the identity provider through SCIM to every downstream app or a ghost account survives. A useful map is the smallest one that still shows those hand-offs and where they break — identity → role → workflow → integration → audit → governance — with a boundary you can defend.

business-system-map.code:
# Business System Map — SaaS Rollout Decision Packet

## Constraint
- Non-negotiable: a terminated user MUST lose all SaaS access promptly on offboarding. SOC 2 CC6.3 requires that access be removed on role change/termination but sets no fixed deadline; the 24h SLA is our internal policy.

## System Map (six layers, directed)
[HR] --lifecycle event--> [IdP: SAML/OIDC] --SSO--> [Salesforce]
         (source of truth)        |
                                   +--SCIM--> [Salesforce RBAC]  (DEprovision lags here)
[Approvals] --elevates--> [Salesforce]        [Salesforce] --events--> [Audit Log]
- Suspect boundary: IdP term event -> SCIM -> app role revocation
- Blast radius if it fails: ghost account keeps live access + record edits; NO data loss
- Out of scope (defended): billing + marketing tools — nothing on this path grants them

## Selected approach
- Drive deprovisioning from HR term event via SCIM (single source of truth)

## Rejected approach
- Manual offboarding checklist per app — bypassed under load, no audit trail

## Inspection-hook outputs (attach)
- RBAC matrix diff: 3 roles grant record export; only 1 was approved
- SCIM provisioning event replay: term event fired, revoke event NEVER acked by app

## Expected failure / verification / reviewer objection / repair notes / capstone connection
steps: Predict the access, workflow, or audit decision before executing.

The hard constraint first: Name the non-negotiable before the solution — here a 24h deprovision SLA (our own target) that satisfies the deprovisioning obligation in SOC 2 CC6.3, which mandates removing access but sets no time window. It must rule out at least one option, or it is decoration.
Source of truth → identity: HR is the system of record; the IdP consumes lifecycle events. If HR never fires the term event, every downstream layer is blind.
The suspect boundary: SSO controls LOGIN; SCIM controls what you can DO and whether you are removed. Deprovisioning lag lives on this async edge — the most common ghost-account cause.
Blast radius: Wrong access + live record edits, but no data loss. Stale-access vs data-loss shapes how loud the incident is.
Defended boundary: Billing and marketing are OUT — and you can say why: nothing on this provisioning path touches them.
Inspection-hook evidence: An RBAC matrix diff and a SCIM event replay turn 'looks fine' into proof: the revoke event fired but the app never acknowledged it.
Change one owner, role, lifecycle, retry, mapping, or evidence assumption and identify the required repair.

storyboard.say: Everything starts in HR: a hire, a role change, or a termination fires an identity lifecycle event into the Identity Provider.
The Identity Provider is the front door. It authenticates the person into Salesforce with an SSO SAML assertion.
In parallel, the IdP tells SCIM to provision or deprovision the account — this is the automation meant to grant and revoke.
SCIM grants the RBAC role inside Salesforce. But on termination this sync LAGS — the revoke never lands, so access stays live.
Separately, the Approval Workflow can elevate access — a second door that also has to be cleaned up on offboarding.
Salesforce emits every access event to the Audit Log — the evidence trail that eventually caught the ghost account.
The blast radius: six teams each owned one layer, nobody owned the map, so the contractor stayed live ninety days.

business-system-map.text: The senior tell in enterprise SaaS is separating authentication from authorization on the map. SSO (SAML/OIDC) proves who you are; SCIM and RBAC decide what you can do and when you are removed. Most 'user has wrong access' incidents are not login failures — they are provisioning-layer drift that a login-only map cannot even see.

business-system-map.question: A terminated employee's SSO login was disabled the day they left, yet an audit finds they still had live edit access in Salesforce for 90 days. Reading the business system map, where is the failure most likely?
options: The SAML assertion was misconfigured, so SSO never worked.
The SCIM deprovisioning event on the IdP → app boundary never completed, so the app-side RBAC role was never revoked even though login was blocked.
The audit log was turned off, so no events were recorded.
The HR system is not the source of truth and should be replaced.
business-system-map.explanation: Disabling SSO stops future LOGINS but does not revoke an already-provisioned RBAC role or kill an active session/API token. Removal travels on the SCIM deprovisioning edge; if that async event never acks at the app, the account keeps its access. That boundary — not the SAML login path — is the suspect edge, and a SCIM event replay is exactly the inspection hook that catches it.

admin-vs-builder-boundary.proof: enterprise_saas_governance_and_integration_packet.md with a constraint table, selected approach (admin vs builder), rejected approach, expected failure, verification method (an OIDC/SAML/SCIM/RBAC inspection hook), and one reviewer objection. A peer can point to the constraint and say why this change sits on the admin side or the builder side.
admin-vs-builder-boundary.unlock: Your packet names the constraint, places the change on the admin or builder side, records the rejected side, and attaches one inspection-hook output — no abstract 'best practices'.
admin-vs-builder-boundary.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'drew the boundary' if your packet only describes what an admin does vs what a builder does. Describing the two roles is not deciding a case. The boundary is a ruling on THIS change, with the failure it prevents (wrong access, drifted records, bypassed approval, incomplete audit).

admin-vs-builder-boundary.text: The VP wants Slack to auto-provision new hires into the finance workspace by Friday. One engineer opens the SCIM connector config; another starts writing a custom provisioning service against the SCIM API. Same request, two totally different blast radii — and nobody has said which side of the line this actually belongs on.

Every enterprise SaaS rollout touches identity, approvals, integrations, audit logs, and reporting — and every change is either admin configuration (governed, reversible, inside the vendor's guardrails) or builder code (custom, powerful, and yours to audit forever). This lesson is Section 1 of the governance packet you carry through the module: the ruling that decides who owns a change and how it can fail.

admin-vs-builder-boundary.prompt: "Marketing needs a field on the Lead object, so we'll build a microservice that writes to the CRM via its API." Before you debate the service design — what is wrong with treating this as a builder task? Answer before reading on.
admin-vs-builder-boundary.reveal: It jumped the boundary. Adding a field is native admin config: the vendor already governs it with validation, audit, and RBAC. A custom writer service throws that away — now YOU own the audit trail, the access checks, and the record-drift risk the platform used to handle for free. The tell of a boundary error: you're rebuilding a governance feature the SaaS already ships. Builder work is for what config genuinely cannot express, not for what's merely faster to script.

# Enterprise SaaS Governance & Integration Packet

## 1. Boundary Ruling — new-hire finance access
- Change: auto-grant Finance workspace to new hires from the HRIS
- Constraint (non-negotiable): every access grant must appear in the audit log
- Selected side: ADMIN — SCIM provisioning + RBAC group mapping
- Rejected side: BUILDER — custom provisioning service via SCIM API
- Why rejected: custom code re-owns audit + access checks SCIM ships free
- Expected failure if wrong: users get incorrect access; audit evidence incomplete
- Verification: SCIM provisioning event replay + RBAC matrix diff
- Reviewer objection: "prove the grant is logged, not just applied"
steps: Predict the access, workflow, or audit decision before executing.
The header: One packet threads the module — identity, approvals, integrations, audit — grown a section per lesson.
Name the change, not the fix: State the business ask. If this line already says 'build a service', you pre-decided the builder side.
The constraint that forces the call: The non-negotiable — here, auditability. It must rule out at least one side, or it is decoration.
Selected and rejected side: Pick admin or builder AND record the loser. A ruling with no rejected side is a preference, not a decision.
Why the rejected side fails: Custom code inherits audit + access + drift ownership the governed surface handled for free. Name what you'd be re-owning.
The feared failure: Specific enough to spot in evidence: incorrect access, record drift, bypassed approval, incomplete audit.
Verification + objection: Attach a real inspection hook (SCIM replay, RBAC diff) and the reviewer challenge it must survive.
Change one owner, role, lifecycle, retry, mapping, or evidence assumption and identify the required repair.

Builder = custom code past that surface (APIs, integrations, webhooks). The invariant: stay admin until config provably cannot express the requirement — because crossing the line moves audit, access, and drift ownership onto you.

storyboard.say: The VP wants Slack auto-provisioning by Friday — one change request enters the control plane, and nobody has said which side of the line it lands on.
Every request first hits the boundary ruling — the single decision that sets the blast radius and decides who owns this change forever.
Ask: is this identity? Then it's SSO via OIDC or SAML — declarative admin config inside the vendor's governed surface.
Is it user lifecycle? SCIM provisioning stays admin — the connector config handles onboarding without a line of custom code.
Is it access or approval? RBAC and workflow are still admin — reversible, governed, inside the guardrails.
Only when config provably cannot express the requirement do you cross to custom code past the API — powerful, and now yours to own.
The split shows in the audit log: admin actions are logged automatically, but builder code must emit its own audit — that's the invariant.
So stay admin until it's impossible — crossing the line moves audit, access, and drift ownership onto you.

# Enterprise SaaS Governance & Integration Packet

## 1. Boundary Ruling — new-hire finance access
- Change: auto-grant Finance workspace to new hires from the HRIS
- Constraint (non-negotiable): every access grant must appear in the audit log
- Selected side: ADMIN — SCIM provisioning + RBAC group mapping
- Rejected side: BUILDER — custom provisioning service via SCIM API
- Why rejected: custom code re-owns audit + access checks SCIM ships free
- Expected failure if wrong: users get incorrect access; audit evidence incomplete
- Verification: SCIM provisioning event replay + RBAC matrix diff
- Reviewer objection: "prove the grant is logged, not just applied"

admin-vs-builder-boundary.text: The senior tell in enterprise SaaS: before writing a line of integration code, ask 'does the vendor already govern this?' A staff admin can name what SCIM, RBAC, and native workflow give for free — audit, access checks, provisioning lifecycle — and refuses to rebuild them in code. Every governance feature you re-implement past the API is a feature you now own the vendor-risk and audit burden for, forever.

admin-vs-builder-boundary.question: A reviewer challenges: which of these change requests is correctly ruled BUILDER (custom code), not ADMIN (config)?
options: "New hires in the HRIS should automatically get the Sales role." — belongs to SCIM + RBAC mapping.
"Managers must approve any access above read-only." — belongs to native workflow/approval config.
"Merge two vendor systems into one nightly reconciled ledger with custom conflict rules no product supports." — no config surface expresses it.
"Add a 'Region' field to the Account object." — belongs to native admin field config.
admin-vs-builder-boundary.explanation: Only option 3 is past the guardrail: no vendor config surface expresses cross-system reconciliation with bespoke conflict rules, so it legitimately becomes builder code — and you accept ownership of its audit trail and integration event log. Options 1, 2, and 4 all map to governed admin surfaces (SCIM/RBAC, workflow, native fields); building custom code for them re-owns audit and access the platform already handles, and invites record drift and bypassed approvals.

record-ownership.outcome: Take one real record that lives in three or more SaaS systems (a user, a role grant, a customer) and write the System of Record decision: which single system owns each field, which way it syncs, and what breaks when a downstream copy disagrees. Solution-free naming of the constraint first.
record-ownership.proof: Section of enterprise_saas_governance_and_integration_packet.md: a field-level ownership table (system of record per field), SCIM/SAML sync direction, the invalidation condition, and one reviewer objection answered. A peer traces one field from its owner to every consumer and agrees no two systems both claim to own it.
record-ownership.unlock: Your packet names one system of record per field, marks sync direction, and states the exact condition under which ownership is violated — with zero fields owned by two systems.
record-ownership.doNotClaim: Do not claim record ownership is defined because you drew arrows between systems. Arrows without a named owner-per-field are integration wallpaper. If two systems can both write the same field with no precedence rule, you have drift waiting to happen, not ownership.

record-ownership.text: A terminated employee still has admin in the billing app three weeks after HR marked them gone — because HR owns the identity, Okta owns the login, and the billing app owns its own local roles, and no one wrote down who wins. The audit finds it before the security team does.

In an enterprise SaaS estate, the same record (a user, a role, an account) exists as copies across the IdP, the HR system, the app, and the audit log. Record ownership is the decision of which system holds the canonical truth for each field — the boundary that stops access errors, silent drift, and incomplete audit evidence.

record-ownership.prompt: "HR, Okta, and the app all store the user's department, and we sync all three both ways so they stay consistent." Before you praise the consistency — what is wrong with that design? Answer before reading on.
record-ownership.reveal: Bidirectional sync between three copies has no source of truth — it has three, which means it has none. When two systems disagree, there is no rule for who wins, so the last writer silently overwrites the truth and you get drift you cannot audit. Real ownership names ONE system of record per field and makes every other copy read-only downstream. "Keep them consistent" is a wish; "HR owns department, Okta and the app are read-only consumers" is a decision.

record-ownership.intro: Trace one controlled and one silently drifting record ownership outcome before editing the TODO.
record-ownership.setup: Take one real record that lives in three or more SaaS systems (a user, a role grant, a customer) and write the System of Record decision: which single system owns each field, which way it syncs, and what breaks when a downstream copy disagrees. record-ownership.code:
## System of Record (per field)
| field            | system of record | consumers (read-only)   | sync         | precedence |
|------------------|------------------|-------------------------|--------------|------------|
| identity/status  | HR (Workday)     | Okta, App, Billing      | SCIM one-way | HR wins    |
| department       | HR (Workday)     | Okta, App               | SCIM one-way | HR wins    |
| auth / SSO group | Okta             | App, Billing            | SAML assert  | Okta wins  |
| app-local role   | App              | (none)                  | app-only     | App wins   |
| audit event      | Audit store      | SIEM (read)             | append-only  | immutable  |
- Invalidation: any field writable in two systems, OR a deprovision in HR that
  does not revoke Okta + App access within the SLA (SCIM deprovision replay proves it).
- Rejected: bidirectional department sync HR<->App (no precedence -> last-writer drift).
- Reviewer objection: "prove deprovision propagates" -> SCIM event replay + RBAC matrix diff attached.
steps: Predict the access, workflow, or audit decision before executing.
One row per field, not per system: Ownership is decided at the FIELD level. A user record is not owned by one system — each of its fields has its own system of record.
HR owns lifecycle: Identity status and department flow one-way out of HR via SCIM. Every downstream copy is read-only. HR wins on conflict — that precedence column is the whole decision.
The IdP owns auth, not identity: Okta owns SSO group membership via SAML assertion; it does NOT own who the person is. Separating auth-ownership from identity-ownership is the senior move.
The app owns only what is truly local: App-local roles are the ONE thing the app is allowed to own. Everything else it merely holds a copy of. Keep this list ruthlessly short.
Audit is append-only, owned by nobody who can edit it: The audit store owns the event trail and no system can rewrite it. Immutable ownership is what makes the evidence trustworthy.
The invalidation condition: State exactly what makes this design wrong: a two-writer field, or a deprovision that doesn't propagate in time. A SCIM deprovision replay is the executable proof.
Rejected option + reviewer objection: Name the bidirectional-sync option you rejected and why, then attach the SCIM replay + RBAC matrix diff that answers the reviewer's challenge.
Change one owner, role, lifecycle, retry, mapping, or evidence assumption and identify the required repair.

A peer traces one field from its owner to every consumer and agrees no two systems both claim to own it.

record-ownership.title: The record-ownership map for a user identity
record-ownership.subtitle: HR owns lifecycle, the IdP owns authentication, the app owns app-local roles, the audit store owns the immutable log. SCIM flows one-way from the owner; the failure edge (app writes its own department back) is marked. Bidirectional sync is deliberately out of scope.

storyboard.say: Ownership starts at HR: it holds the canonical lifecycle for this identity — who exists, and whether they are still employed.
HR feeds identity to Okta, the IdP, which owns authentication — it decides who can log in, but not what HR decides.
Okta pushes provisioning through SCIM: a SAML assertion plus a one-way sync that fans identity out to downstream apps.
The SaaS app receives a read-only copy. It owns its app-local roles, but the identity fields it holds are downstream, not canonical.
Here is the risk: the app writes its own department override locally, creating a second writer for a field HR already owns.
That local write bleeding back toward HR violates the system of record — two writers means drift, and drift is untrustworthy truth.
Both Okta and the app emit events to the immutable audit store, which owns the log — and it is what catches the drift first.
The invariant: name exactly one owner per field, feed every copy one-way, and never let a field be writable in two places.

## System of Record (per field)
| field            | system of record | consumers (read-only)   | sync         | precedence |
|------------------|------------------|-------------------------|--------------|------------|
| identity/status  | HR (Workday)     | Okta, App, Billing      | SCIM one-way | HR wins    |
| department       | HR (Workday)     | Okta, App               | SCIM one-way | HR wins    |
| auth / SSO group | Okta             | App, Billing            | SAML assert  | Okta wins  |
| app-local role   | App              | (none)                  | app-only     | App wins   |
| audit event      | Audit store      | SIEM (read)             | append-only  | immutable  |
- Invalidation: any field writable in two systems, OR a deprovision in HR that
  does not revoke Okta + App access within the SLA (SCIM deprovision replay proves it).
- Rejected: bidirectional department sync HR<->App (no precedence -> last-writer drift).
- Reviewer objection: "prove deprovision propagates" -> SCIM event replay + RBAC matrix diff attached.

steps.label: One row per field, not per system
steps.note: Ownership is decided at the FIELD level. A user record is not owned by one system — each of its fields has its own system of record.

steps.label: HR owns lifecycle
steps.note: Identity status and department flow one-way out of HR via SCIM. Every downstream copy is read-only. HR wins on conflict — that precedence column is the whole decision.

steps.label: The IdP owns auth, not identity
steps.note: Okta owns SSO group membership via SAML assertion; it does NOT own who the person is. Separating auth-ownership from identity-ownership is the senior move.

steps.label: The app owns only what is truly local
steps.note: App-local roles are the ONE thing the app is allowed to own. Everything else it merely holds a copy of. Keep this list ruthlessly short.

steps.label: Audit is append-only, owned by nobody who can edit it
steps.note: The audit store owns the event trail and no system can rewrite it. Immutable ownership is what makes the evidence trustworthy.

steps.label: The invalidation condition
steps.note: State exactly what makes this design wrong: a two-writer field, or a deprovision that doesn't propagate in time. A SCIM deprovision replay is the executable proof.

workflow-lifecycle.text: Six months after a clean SaaS rollout, an auditor pulls the access report and finds a contractor who left in March still provisioned in the billing system, approved by a manager who no longer exists. Nothing broke on launch day — the lifecycle broke quietly, one un-triggered deprovisioning event at a time.

An enterprise SaaS system is not configured once; every user and record moves through a lifecycle — requested, approved, provisioned, synced, audited, revoked. Release or review risk lives in the transitions nobody watches, so this lesson's artifact is a lifecycle map whose failure points a reviewer can replay.

workflow-lifecycle.prompt: "SSO works and new hires can log in — the rollout is done." Before you agree: what part of the workflow lifecycle did that sentence not test at all? Answer before reading on.
workflow-lifecycle.reveal: It tested exactly one transition: provision → authenticate. It says nothing about approval (did the right person authorize this access?), sync (does the record match the source of truth across systems?), audit (is there an inspectable trail?), or deprovisioning (does access end when employment does?). "They can log in" is the one stage that always gets tested because it's visible. The lifecycle fails at the transitions that only surface at audit — a SCIM deprovision event that never fired, an RBAC role that drifted, an approval that was auto-granted.

# Enterprise SaaS Governance & Integration Packet

## 1. Lifecycle stages (the workflow, end-to-end)
request -> approval -> SCIM provision -> RBAC role -> audit log -> deprovision

## 2. Constraint (non-negotiable)
Offboarding MUST revoke all access promptly (our target: within 24h). This maps to SOC 2 CC6.3's requirement to remove access on termination, which specifies no fixed deadline.

## 3. Selected approach
Drive lifecycle from the IdP: SCIM push provisions AND deprovisions the SaaS app.

## 4. Rejected approach
Manual ticket to revoke access on offboard — breaks under release/review risk:
the ticket is the transition nobody fires, so access outlives employment.

## 5. Expected failure
IdP offboard event does not propagate: SCIM deprovision never reaches the app;
orphaned account keeps its RBAC role; audit log shows no revoke event.

## 6. Verification (inspection hooks)
- [ ] SCIM provisioning event replay: replay an offboard, confirm deprovision fires
- [ ] RBAC matrix diff: compare IdP roles vs SaaS roles — zero drift, zero orphans

## 7. Reviewer objection + answer
Objection: "Is deprovisioning PROVEN or just configured?"
Answer: attached replay log + RBAC diff showing the March contractor now revoked.

Map the full lifecycle: Six stages, not three. If deprovisioning and audit are missing, the lifecycle can't fail in the place it actually fails — you've drawn the demo path.

The hard constraint: Offboard revokes within 24h. This maps to SOC 2 CC6.3 (removing access on termination) — the design must actually enforce revocation, not just document intent, or it is decoration. SOC 2 does not mandate automation over a manual approach.
Selected vs rejected: IdP-driven SCIM deprovisioning vs a manual revoke ticket. The rejected option fails precisely because its transition is human-triggered — the one nobody fires.
Name the expected failure: Not 'something breaks' — the specific chain: offboard → SCIM silent → orphaned RBAC role → no audit event. This is the failure the diagram's dashed edge warns about.
Two inspection hooks, executable: SCIM provisioning event replay + RBAC matrix diff. Each can return 'no' and expose the orphan — a hook that can only confirm is theater.
Answer the reviewer, with evidence: The objection is always 'proven or described?'. The answer is the attached replay log + diff, not a paragraph.
Change one owner, role, lifecycle, retry, mapping, or evidence assumption and identify the required repair.

workflow-lifecycle.subtitle: A user record travels request → approval → SCIM provisioning → cross-system sync → audit log → deprovisioning. The suspect edge is the deprovisioning trigger; the blast radius is orphaned access that only surfaces at audit. SAML auth and the source-of-truth IdP are on the trusted path.

legend.label: deprovisioning — the transition that silently fails

storyboard.say: Every access starts as a request that routes to an approval gate, where a human decides whether the user should ever get in.
On approve, the request grants at the Identity Provider, our source of truth, and the same moment writes who approved, when, and why to the audit log.
The IdP fires a provisioning event to SCIM, which creates the account and role in the SaaS app and logs that it did so.
So far every transition leaves inspectable evidence in the audit log — that is the invariant this lifecycle is supposed to hold.
Here is the suspect edge: when someone leaves, the IdP should trigger deprovisioning to revoke their SaaS access.
But this transition emits no audit event, so if offboarding never fires, nothing breaks and nothing is logged — the access just silently drifts.
Months later the auditor replays the map and finds the orphan: still provisioned, approved by a manager who no longer exists. A transition with no audit event is where access hides.

SSO that only handles login, never deprovisioning, is a badge reader on a door with no lock on the window.

Rolling out a SaaS system means deciding how identity, roles, provisioning, and audit evidence flow between your IdP and the vendor. This lesson turns 'we turned on SSO' into a reviewable Decision Packet — the artifact every later Identity & Access lesson in this module builds on.

saml-oidc-sso.reveal: Provisioning and deprovisioning. SAML/OIDC only prove WHO is logging in at the moment of login (authentication). They do nothing about creating the account, assigning its role, or deleting it when the person leaves — that is SCIM's job. A SAML-only rollout leaves orphaned accounts, local passwords that bypass the IdP, and roles set by hand in the vendor UI. The org drifts: the IdP says a user is gone, the SaaS app says they can still sign in.

# SaaS SSO/Provisioning Decision Packet — Billing SaaS (Chargebee-class)

## 1. Constraint
- Non-negotiable: terminated user loses ALL access within 15 min of HR status change
- Regulatory: SOX audit needs a login + role-grant trail per user, exportable

## 2. Selected approach
- AuthN: OIDC (Authorization Code + PKCE) via Entra ID as IdP
- Lifecycle: SCIM 2.0 push — create/update/deactivate driven by HR-to-Entra sync
- Roles: 3 RBAC groups (billing_admin, billing_viewer, finance_read) mapped from Entra groups

## 3. Rejected approach
- SAML-only, no SCIM: rejected — deprovisioning would be manual, misses the 15-min SLA
- Local accounts + shared admin: rejected — no per-user audit trail, fails SOX

## 4. Expected failure
- SCIM deactivate silently fails (vendor rate-limits the DELETE) -> orphaned active account

## 5. Verification method (inspection hooks)
- OIDC metadata review: iss + jwks_uri match Entra; id_token aud = our client_id
- SCIM event replay: deactivate test user -> confirm 401 on next login within 15 min
- RBAC matrix diff: Entra group membership == app role, no manual grants
- Audit-log review: export shows login + role-change events, per user, timestamped

## 6. Reviewer objection + repair
- Objection: "prove deprovisioning fires, do not just describe it"
- Repair: attach SCIM replay log + the 401 screenshot to the evidence ledger

saml-oidc-sso.title: The identity flow: login, lifecycle, and the audit trail
saml-oidc-sso.subtitle: The IdP is the source of truth. SAML/OIDC carry the login assertion; SCIM carries the lifecycle (create/update/deactivate); the audit log records both. The suspect edge is SCIM deprovisioning — where terminated access silently survives. Local passwords are the boundary we forbid.

nodes.label: HR / IdP directory
nodes.description: source of truth for identity + role

storyboard.say: It starts at the IdP directory: HR sets each person's role and status, and the Identity Provider becomes the single source of truth.
For login, the IdP issues a SAML or OIDC assertion that answers one question: who is this person, right now?
That assertion carries into the SaaS app and logs the user in — no separate password, just the IdP vouching for them.
Login isn't lifecycle. SCIM is the second channel: the IdP fires create, update, and deactivate events at the connector.
Here's the suspect edge: SCIM must provision AND deprovision. If deprovisioning never fires, terminated access silently survives.
A local password is the forbidden boundary — it's a door that bypasses the IdP entirely, so it must not exist.
Finally the app writes to the audit log — who, when, what role — so login and lifecycle both trace back to one identity.

saml-oidc-sso.text: The senior tell in identity work: never confuse authentication with authorization with lifecycle. SAML/OIDC prove identity at one instant. scim-provisioning.text: An engineer resigned four months ago; today an auditor pulls the SaaS access report and her account in the analytics tool is still active, still licensed, still able to export customer data. The IdP said 'de-provisioned.' Nobody ever checked what SCIM actually did downstream.

SCIM is the protocol that carries identity lifecycle events — create, update, deactivate — from your IdP into every SaaS app, so joiners, movers, and leavers stay in sync automatically. This lesson sits in Identity Access & Provisioning because provisioning is where access correctness is won or lost: when it fails silently, users get wrong access, records drift across systems, and the audit trail cannot prove who could do what, when.

scim-provisioning.prompt: Your IdP dashboard shows the SCIM connection to a SaaS app as 'Connected · Last sync succeeded.' A user was offboarded yesterday. Is that green status enough to tell the auditor their access is gone? Answer before reading on.
scim-provisioning.reveal: No — and this is the failure that hides in plain sight. 'Sync succeeded' means the last batch of SCIM calls returned 2xx, not that the deactivate call for that specific user was sent and honored. SCIM deprovisioning fails silently in three common ways: the IdP maps deactivation to a field the app ignores, the app 'soft-deletes' but keeps the session/API token alive, or the user was assigned directly in the app (out-of-band) so the IdP never had authority to remove them. Access correctness is a per-event claim you replay, never a per-connection status you glance at.

scim-provisioning.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# SCIM provisioning event replay — inspection hook for one leaver.
BASE="https://app.vendor.com/scim/v2"; USER_ID="3f2b-terminated-user"

# 1. Capture RBAC state BEFORE (source-of-truth: this user should be gone)
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $SCIM_TOKEN" \
  "$BASE/Users/$USER_ID" | jq '{active, roles: .roles, groups: .groups}' > before.json

# 2. Replay the exact deactivate the IdP claims it sent
curl -s -X PATCH -H "Authorization: Bearer $SCIM_TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/scim+json' "$BASE/Users/$USER_ID" \
  -d '{"schemas":["urn:ietf:params:scim:api:messages:2.0:PatchOp"],
       "Operations":[{"op":"replace","path":"active","value":false}]}'

# 3. Capture AFTER + confirm the app emitted an audit event
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $SCIM_TOKEN" \
  "$BASE/Users/$USER_ID" | jq '{active, roles: .roles}' > after.json
diff <(jq . before.json) <(jq . after.json)   # <- the RBAC matrix diff

# 4. FAIL the check if active is still true OR no audit line exists
jq -e '.active == false' after.json > /dev/null || echo 'GHOST: still active'
steps: Predict the access, workflow, or audit decision before executing.
Snapshot before: Record the entitlements the leaver still holds. If this returns 404, provisioning already worked — but you must show that, not assume it.
Replay the deactivate: Send the exact SCIM PATCH the IdP logs as 'sent'. Replaying it yourself is what turns 'the IdP says so' into observed behavior.
Diff after vs before: The RBAC matrix diff IS the proof artifact: roles and groups must go to empty/inactive. A diff that shows no change is a ghost account.
The falsifiable check: The script FAILS loud when active is still true. A test that can only pass is theatre — this one can return 'GHOST' and kill the claim.

scim-provisioning.subtitle: HR termination → IdP SCIM deactivate → SaaS app. The suspect edge is IdP → SaaS (the deactivate call); the blast radius is a ghost account with live entitlements. Direct-in-app assignment is the out-of-band drift the IdP cannot see.

storyboard.say: It starts in HR: an engineer resigns, and the HRIS marks her terminated — the single lifecycle event that should ripple everywhere.
The Identity Provider is the source of truth. It receives the termination and fires a SCIM deactivate to every connected SaaS app.
This is the suspect edge. The IdP dashboard says 'de-provisioned' — but that only means the call was attempted, not that it landed.
SCIM sends a PATCH to the SaaS app to flip the user inactive. Everything upstream now looks green.
Here's the silent failure: the app ignores or soft-deletes the request, leaving a ghost account — still active, still licensed, still able to export customer data.
The proof gap: the app SHOULD have logged a revoke to the audit trail. No revoke line means nobody can tell the deactivate never took.
And drift compounds: someone assigned access directly in the app — out of band, invisible to the IdP, which never knew to revoke it.
The invariant: replay one leaver's deactivate from IdP call to account state to entitlements — every app must converge or surface the drift.

rbac-modeling.text: Go-live day for the new SaaS. A support agent opens a ticket, clicks through, and lands on the finance export — full customer PII, every invoice — because 'Support' was mapped to a role that quietly inherited 'read: billing'. Nobody modeled it; someone just cloned an existing role and shipped.

RBAC is where identity turns into consequence: SSO says who you are, SCIM provisions the account, but the role model decides what you can touch. Model it shallow and users get incorrect access, records drift across systems, approvals get bypassed, and the audit trail cannot answer 'who could have done this' — this is Section 2 of the governance packet you carry through this module.

rbac-modeling.prompt: 'Just give the new hires the Manager role so they aren't blocked.' Before you agree — what is wrong with that as an access decision? Answer before reading on.
rbac-modeling.reveal: It grants a capability set to solve an onboarding delay — two different problems fused. 'Manager' bundles approve-refunds, export-reports, and edit-billing; the new hire needed exactly one of them. Over-granting to unblock is how least-privilege dies quietly: nothing breaks in the demo, and six months later the audit finds thirty accounts that could issue refunds and never should have. The real constraint was 'ship access without violating least-privilege', not 'unblock the hire'.

rbac-modeling.code:
## 2. RBAC Model
Constraint: least-privilege — no role reads billing PII unless the job task requires it.

| role            | tickets:rw | refunds:approve | billing:read | reports:export | admin:users |
|-----------------|:----------:|:---------------:|:------------:|:--------------:|:-----------:|
| Support Agent   |   ALLOW    |      DENY       |     DENY     |      DENY      |    DENY     |
| Support Lead    |   ALLOW    |   ALLOW (<=$50)  |     DENY     |      DENY      |    DENY     |
| Finance Analyst |    DENY    |      DENY       |    ALLOW     |     ALLOW      |    DENY     |
| IT Admin        |    DENY    |      DENY       |     DENY     |      DENY      |    ALLOW    |

- Selected: task-scoped roles, no inheritance (a Lead is NOT 'Agent + billing')
- Rejected: single 'Manager' role bundling approve + export + billing (over-grants 3 permissions)
- SCIM mapping: IdP group `sso-support` -> role `Support Agent` (verified by provisioning replay)
- Expected failure: role cloned to unblock a hire silently inherits `billing:read`
- Verification: RBAC matrix diff between intended table and live grants -> zero unexplained ALLOWs
steps: Predict the access, workflow, or audit decision before executing.

Name the constraint first: Least-privilege is the non-negotiable. State it before the matrix so every grant has to justify itself against it — the source doctrine: name the operating constraint before the solution.

The Support Agent row: Four DENYs and one ALLOW. This is the model working: the agent from the mission can touch tickets and nothing else. billing:read is DENY on purpose, and you can point to the cell.

Scoped elevation, not a new tier: Support Lead adds ONE capability (refunds up to $50), it does not inherit Agent-plus-billing. Bounded elevation is how you avoid role explosion and silent PII access.

Selected vs rejected: The rejected 'Manager' bundle is the mission's bug in a single role. Recording the rejected coarser option is the expert move the source demands — the decision is inspectable, not asserted.

Bind identity to the model via SCIM: The IdP group maps to exactly one role. Provisioning event replay proves sso-support lands on Support Agent and not something wider — identity, provisioning, and RBAC now agree.

Verification is a diff, not a vibe: An RBAC matrix diff between the intended table and live grants must return zero unexplained ALLOWs. That diff is the evidence a reviewer replays — this is where 'described' becomes 'proven'.

rbac-modeling.title: Where the RBAC model sits in the SaaS access path
rbac-modeling.subtitle: IdP proves identity, SCIM provisions the account, the RBAC role model decides capability, and the audit log records every grant. The suspect edge is role-to-permission: over-grant here and the blast radius is a support agent reading finance PII. Payroll config is deliberately out of scope.

legend.label: the suspect edge — role to permission

storyboard.say: The path starts at the Identity Provider: single sign-on proves who the user is, then asserts that identity into SCIM provisioning.
SCIM provisions the account and assigns a role. Identity is settled here, but capability is not yet decided.
The RBAC role model is where identity turns into consequence: it decides exactly which permissions the SaaS app grants.
Here is the suspect edge. A Support role that quietly inherited read-billing lets the app reach the finance export.
Blast radius: a support agent lands on full customer PII and every invoice, because someone cloned a role instead of modeling it.
Every grant the role model makes is written to the audit log, so you can always answer who could have touched what.
The invariant: map each role to the exact permissions it holds and is denied. A grant nobody can explain is drift waiting to happen.

rbac-modeling.text: The senior tell in an access review: a strong RBAC model separates signal from noise — it states what is directly observable (the matrix), what must be inferred (inherited grants), and what would invalidate it (an ALLOW no job task justifies). rbac-modeling.question: A reviewer challenges: 'Prove this RBAC model is least-privilege, not just that it looks reasonable.' Which response is real evidence?
options: 'Every role has a clear name and an owner listed in the wiki.'
'The matrix diff between the intended role-permission table and the live grants returns zero unexplained ALLOWs, and a SCIM provisioning replay shows sso-support lands only on Support Agent.'
'We followed best practices and used the vendor's default roles.'
'No one has complained about their access since launch.'
rbac-modeling.explanation: Only option 2 is inspectable and replayable: a matrix diff proves the live system matches the intended least-privilege table (catching cloned-role drift), and a provisioning-event replay proves identity maps to exactly the intended role. Named owners (1), 'best practices' / vendor defaults (3), and absence of complaints (4) are descriptions and vibes — none can return a 'no' that eliminates the over-grant.

storyboard.say: Everything starts with the source of truth: HR and your identity provider define who is intended to have what, encoded as an RBAC matrix.
The matrix is only intent. The review pulls actual entitlements straight from SSO and SCIM — what people can really touch right now.
Both sides feed the diff: expected access from the matrix, observed access from the systems. The review IS this comparison.
Every mismatch is drift — the contractor still holding billing admin — and each one is routed to an explicit decision, not a signed spreadsheet.
The decision does two things at once: it writes the evidence to the audit log so the resolution is provable later.
And it writes back to reality — revoking or deprovisioning the entitlement so the actual state finally matches the intended one.
The failure path: an approval bypass grants access unseen, skipping the diff and the log. That silent grant is exactly what an auditor cannot explain.

approval-flow.unlock: Your decision names the enforcement point, records the rejected option, and attaches one audit-trail line that proves the approval gate actually blocked provisioning — not just that a UI showed an approve button.
approval-flow.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have an approval flow if the approval is advisory — a notification a manager can ignore while SCIM still provisions access. A gate that cannot deny is theater. The flow must be able to return 'denied' and stop provisioning.

approval-flow.text: A contractor requests admin on the finance SaaS, the manager clicks approve on autopilot, SCIM provisions the role in ninety seconds — and four months later the SOX auditor asks for the approval record and finds a Slack thumbs-up nobody can tie to the grant. The access was real; the control was a costume.

This is the first lesson of Business Process Automation, and approval flow is the boundary-and-ownership control the whole module rests on. It converts 'someone said yes' into an enforced, inspectable gate between an access request and the identity systems (SAML, SCIM, RBAC) that actually grant power.

approval-flow.prompt: "We added an approval step: the manager gets an email and clicks Approve before we grant the role." Before you ship that — what is wrong with it as an approval FLOW? Answer before reading on.
approval-flow.reveal: Nothing enforces the 'before'. If SCIM provisioning runs on the request event and the email is just a parallel notification, access is live whether or not the manager ever clicks — the approval is decorative. A real approval flow makes the grant DEPEND on the decision: no approver state = no provisioning, and the deny path is a first-class outcome that leaves an audit record. Naming an approver feels like a control while quietly changing nothing about who gets access.

approval-flow.code:
# enterprise_saas_governance_and_integration_packet.md -> approval_flow.yaml
flow: contractor_admin_grant
trigger: access_request.created         # scope: role=finance_admin
constraint: SOX 404 - privileged grants require recorded prior approval

steps:
  - id: approval_gate
    type: approval
    approver: requester.manager          # not the requester (SoD)
    on_deny: stop                        # deny is a real outcome
    timeout: 24h -> auto_deny            # no silent auto-grant

  - id: provision
    type: scim.grant_role
    depends_on: approval_gate.state == APPROVED   # the enforcement point
    role: finance_admin

audit:
  write: [approval_gate.decision, approval_gate.actor, provision.result]
  fields: [request_id, decision, actor, timestamp, role]
  immutable: true
steps: Predict the access, workflow, or audit decision before executing.

approval-flow.title: The approval flow as an enforced access gate
approval-flow.subtitle: Access request enters the workflow engine; the approval gate is a decision that BLOCKS provisioning until an approver state is recorded. Approve routes to SCIM/SAML provisioning + audit; deny stops the grant and still writes an audit line. Billing and reporting are deliberately out of scope.

legend.label: the gate on the critical path
the invariant: no decision, no access

storyboard.say: A requester submits an access request — say a contractor asking for admin on the finance SaaS — and it enters the workflow engine.
The engine does not grant anything yet. Every request must pass through the approval gate first — that is the whole point.
The gate is a hard decision on the critical path: with no recorded approver state, there is simply no grant.
On an explicit approve, the gate routes to SCIM and SAML provisioning, which actually assigns the role in the identity systems.
That grant writes an inspectable audit line — four months later the SOX auditor sees the record, not a Slack thumbs-up.
A deny must genuinely stop the grant — access denied, no role provisioned — and it still writes its own audit line.
Enforcement, reversibility, and evidence together: the approver sits between request and power, and every decision is inspectable.

approval-flow.title: The approval flow as config — SCIM provisioning gated on a recorded decision
approval-flow.subtitle: A workflow definition the reviewer can read: the grant step DEPENDS on the approval step's recorded state, and both outcomes write to the audit log.
approval-flow.code:
# enterprise_saas_governance_and_integration_packet.md -> approval_flow.yaml
flow: contractor_admin_grant
trigger: access_request.created         # scope: role=finance_admin
constraint: SOX 404 - privileged grants require recorded prior approval

steps:
  - id: approval_gate
    type: approval
    approver: requester.manager          # not the requester (SoD)
    on_deny: stop                        # deny is a real outcome
    timeout: 24h -> auto_deny            # no silent auto-grant

    type: scim.grant_role
    depends_on: approval_gate.state == APPROVED   # the enforcement point
    role: finance_admin

audit:
  write: [approval_gate.decision, approval_gate.actor, provision.result]
  fields: [request_id, decision, actor, timestamp, role]
  immutable: true

ticketing-workflow.text: Audit week: the assessor pulls one ticket — "Grant Priya admin on Billing" — and asks a single question, "Who approved this, and does the log agree?" The ticket says APPROVED. The SSO logs say Priya had admin four days before the ticket opened. The room goes quiet, because the workflow recorded the decision but never controlled it.

In a SaaS rollout, access is granted hundreds of times across identity, RBAC, and integrations. The ticketing workflow is where an access request either becomes an inspectable, policy-bound control — or a rubber stamp that drifts from what the systems actually did. This is the second lesson in Business Process Automation: it turns "we have a form" into "we have provable governance."

ticketing-workflow.prompt: A ticket reads: "Approved by manager — granted admin to Finance app." It is closed, timestamped, and signed. Before you call it compliant — what is missing? Answer before reading on.
ticketing-workflow.reveal: It proves a decision was made, not that the control held. Missing: WHICH policy the manager was authorized to approve against (a manager can't self-authorize privileged roles), and whether the SCIM/SAML provisioning event MATCHES the ticket — same user, same role, same time. A ticket that closes without a linked audit event is a claim, not evidence. Real ticketing binds request → approval → provisioning event → audit log so the four agree or the exception is flagged.

ticketing-workflow.code:
# ticketing_workflow.yaml — access-request control for the Finance SaaS
workflow: saas_access_request
identity_source: okta_saml        # SSO is the one source of truth for who
provisioning: scim_v2             # every grant flows through SCIM, never by hand

role_tiers:
  standard:  { approver: line_manager,        sla_hours: 24 }
  sensitive: { approver: data_owner,          sla_hours: 8, mfa_step_up: true }
  admin:     { approver: [data_owner, security_lead], sla_hours: 4, dual_control: true }

rules:
  - id: no_self_approve
    assert: request.requester_id != approval.approver_id
  - id: tier_authority
    assert: approval.approver in role_tiers[request.tier].approver
  - id: reconcile_grant       # THE control: log must match the ticket
    assert: scim.grant.role == ticket.role AND scim.grant.user == ticket.user
    on_fail: flag('unprovable_grant') and open_incident

audit:
  emit: [ticket_id, requester, approver, tier, scim_event_id, granted_at]
  drift_scan: daily            # any app role with no approved ticket => alert
steps: Predict the access, workflow, or audit decision before executing.
Anchor identity + provisioning: SAML is the only source of truth for identity; every grant flows through SCIM. Hand-edits in the app have no ticket — the drift scan will surface them.

Tier the approval, not just the request: Standard access ≠ admin. Admin demands dual_control (two approvers) and step-up MFA. Uniform routing is exactly how approvals get bypassed for the risky grants.
no_self_approve + tier_authority: A requester cannot approve their own access, and only an approver authorized for that tier can sign. This is the RBAC-matrix diff made executable.

reconcile_grant — the actual control: The SCIM provisioning event must match the ticket's user and role. If they disagree, the grant is 'unprovable' and opens an incident. This is what turns a form into a control.
Emit + daily drift scan: The audit event carries the scim_event_id so ticket and log are linkable forever. The daily scan finds any live role with no approved ticket — the back door in the diagram.
Change one owner, role, lifecycle, retry, mapping, or evidence assumption and identify the required repair.

A second reviewer can replay one denied request end-to-end without you narrating.

storyboard.say: It starts here: a requester opens an access ticket — grant Priya admin on Billing — the trigger for the whole control chain.
The ticket routes by role tier into the approval gate — the policy-checked control where a human or rule must actually decide.
On approve, the gate triggers the SCIM provisioner, which combines the request with the IdP's identity assertion.
SCIM provisions the role into the SaaS app, and the app emits a grant event into the audit log.
The keystone control: the ticket reconciles against the log — does an approved ticket exist for every grant the systems recorded?
Here's the bypass: a direct grant provisions the app with no ticket at all — access exists that the workflow never approved.
Reconcile is what catches it: Priya had admin four days before the ticket opened, so log and ticket disagree — drift, exposed.
The invariant: if ticket and log can disagree silently, you have a form, not a control. The chain must be reconstructable evidence.

ticketing-workflow.title: The workflow-as-config the reviewer inspects
ticketing-workflow.subtitle: Tiered approval routing + a reconciliation rule that flags any grant with no matching approved ticket — the artifact's executable core.
ticketing-workflow.code:
# ticketing_workflow.yaml — access-request control for the Finance SaaS
workflow: saas_access_request
identity_source: okta_saml        # SSO is the one source of truth for who
provisioning: scim_v2             # every grant flows through SCIM, never by hand

role_tiers:
  standard:  { approver: line_manager,        sla_hours: 24 }
  sensitive: { approver: data_owner,          sla_hours: 8, mfa_step_up: true }
  admin:     { approver: [data_owner, security_lead], sla_hours: 4, dual_control: true }

rules:
  - id: no_self_approve
    assert: request.requester_id != approval.approver_id
  - id: tier_authority
    assert: approval.approver in role_tiers[request.tier].approver
  - id: reconcile_grant       # THE control: log must match the ticket
    assert: scim.grant.role == ticket.role AND scim.grant.user == ticket.user
    on_fail: flag('unprovable_grant') and open_incident

audit:
  emit: [ticket_id, requester, approver, tier, scim_event_id, granted_at]
  drift_scan: daily            # any app role with no approved ticket => alert

steps.label: Anchor identity + provisioning
steps.note: SAML is the only source of truth for identity; every grant flows through SCIM. Hand-edits in the app have no ticket — the drift scan will surface them.

steps.label: Tier the approval, not just the request
steps.note: Standard access ≠ admin. Admin demands dual_control (two approvers) and step-up MFA. Uniform routing is exactly how approvals get bypassed for the risky grants.

steps.label: no_self_approve + tier_authority
steps.note: A requester cannot approve their own access, and only an approver authorized for that tier can sign. This is the RBAC-matrix diff made executable.

steps.label: reconcile_grant — the actual control
steps.note: The SCIM provisioning event must match the ticket's user and role. If they disagree, the grant is 'unprovable' and opens an incident. This is what turns a form into a control.

steps.label: Emit + daily drift scan
steps.note: The audit event carries the scim_event_id so ticket and log are linkable forever. The daily scan finds any live role with no approved ticket — the back door in the diagram.

ticketing-workflow.text: The senior tell in enterprise IT: an auditor doesn't ask 'do you have an approval process?' — they pull ONE ticket and ask you to prove the grant from the log. If your evidence is the ticket describing itself, you have circular proof. Real governance means the audit trail can reconstruct the grant WITHOUT trusting the ticket. Bind request → approval → SCIM event → audit log, and separation-of-duties (no self-approve, tiered authority) is enforced before provisioning, not reviewed after.

ticketing-workflow.question: A reviewer challenges your ticketing workflow: "Show me this grant is proven, not just described." Which evidence actually answers that?
options: The closed ticket, showing the manager clicked Approve and added a comment.
The audit event linking ticket_id → approver (authorized for that tier) → the matching SCIM provisioning event, plus a drift scan showing no un-ticketed grants.
A screenshot of the user now able to log into the app.
The policy document stating that admin access requires approval.

crm-itsm-patterns.text: Go-live morning: the new ITSM platform is up, tickets are flowing — and a contractor who left in March still has admin, because the CRM sync never revoked her and no one replayed the SCIM feed. Nobody described the access wrong; nobody proved it right.

A CRM/ITSM rollout is where identity, approvals, integrations, audit logs, and reporting all touch the same records at once — so the failure is never one bug, it is drift across systems. This lesson turns 'we configured it' into an inspectable packet a reviewer can replay, the same evidence artifact your capstone reuses.

crm-itsm-patterns.prompt: A rollout review asks: 'Is access correct?' and the admin answers 'Yes — the RBAC roles are configured per the design.' What is wrong with that answer before you even check the roles?
crm-itsm-patterns.reveal: It proves the design, not the running system. 'Configured per the design' is a claim about intent; access correctness is a claim about state — who can actually do what right now, after CRM created the user, SCIM provisioned them, SAML asserted their groups, and an approval (maybe) gated the elevation. The gap between 'configured' and 'observed' is exactly where the departed contractor keeps her admin. A real answer is an RBAC matrix diff and a SCIM event replay, not a sentence about the design.

crm-itsm-patterns.code:
## Constraint
- Identity lifecycle: CRM is source of truth; ITSM access MUST revoke <=24h after CRM offboard.

## Selected approach
- SCIM push from IdP -> ITSM, with a nightly RBAC matrix diff as the backstop.

## Rejected approach
- Manual role removal by the ITSM admin (no event trail -> silent drift). Rejected: unprovable.

## Verification (inspection hooks — run, not described)
$ scim-replay --user contractor.jane --from 2026-03-01 --event deprovision
  -> 2026-03-14 CRM offboard emitted
  -> 2026-03-14 SCIM DELETE sent to ITSM ...... 200 OK
  -> ITSM role 'incident_admin' STILL PRESENT   <-- FAIL

$ rbac-matrix-diff --baseline design.csv --observed live.csv
  + contractor.jane : incident_admin (not in baseline)   <-- FAIL

## Expected failure + reviewer objection
- Failure: deprovision emitted but ITSM ignored DELETE on active-session roles.
- Reviewer: 'Prove access is revoked, not just that CRM fired the event.'
- Response: the matrix diff above is the observed-state proof; CRM event alone is not.
steps: Predict the access, workflow, or audit decision before executing.
Constraint first, then approach: Name the non-negotiable (revoke <=24h) BEFORE the pattern. A constraint that rules out no option is decoration — this one rules out manual removal.
Selected approach: SCIM push + a nightly RBAC matrix diff backstop. The backstop exists precisely because sync silently fails.

Rejected approach + why: Manual removal is rejected not because it is lazy but because it leaves no event trail — it is unprovable under operational evidence. Recording the rejection is the expert move.
SCIM provisioning event replay: The hook REPLAYS the offboard: CRM fired, SCIM sent DELETE, ITSM returned 200 — yet the role survived. Observed state contradicts the happy path.
RBAC matrix diff: Baseline (design) vs observed (live). The '+' line is the departed contractor still holding incident_admin — the exact go-live failure, caught by evidence, not opinion.

Failure + reviewer objection + response: The invalidation condition: access looks acceptable in review but fails when you replay the deprovision. The response points at observed state, never at the CRM event alone.

storyboard.say: It starts in the CRM, the system of record: a contractor leaves, and that lifecycle event should fire identity changes to the IdP.
The IdP asserts group membership over SAML or OIDC, handing the source of truth to the SCIM sync that provisions accounts.
SCIM provisions roles into the ITSM platform's RBAC — but this sync lags and drops events, so revocations quietly go missing.
Inside ITSM, a privilege elevation hits the approval gate, and every who-what-when decision is written to the audit log.
Here's the blast radius: a missed deprovision or a bypassed gate leaves stale, over-privileged admin access nobody proved was correct.
ITSM still feeds clean-looking records to business reporting — so drift stays invisible in the dashboards downstream.
The lesson: turn 'we configured it' into a replayable evidence packet — an inspectable audit trail that proves access right, not just described.

crm-itsm-patterns.code:
## Constraint
- Identity lifecycle: CRM is source of truth; ITSM access MUST revoke <=24h after CRM offboard.

## Selected approach
- SCIM push from IdP -> ITSM, with a nightly RBAC matrix diff as the backstop.

## Rejected approach
- Manual role removal by the ITSM admin (no event trail -> silent drift). Rejected: unprovable.

## Verification (inspection hooks — run, not described)
$ scim-replay --user contractor.jane --from 2026-03-01 --event deprovision
  -> 2026-03-14 CRM offboard emitted
  -> 2026-03-14 SCIM DELETE sent to ITSM ...... 200 OK
  -> ITSM role 'incident_admin' STILL PRESENT   <-- FAIL

$ rbac-matrix-diff --baseline design.csv --observed live.csv
  + contractor.jane : incident_admin (not in baseline)   <-- FAIL

## Expected failure + reviewer objection
- Failure: deprovision emitted but ITSM ignored DELETE on active-session roles.
- Reviewer: 'Prove access is revoked, not just that CRM fired the event.'
- Response: the matrix diff above is the observed-state proof; CRM event alone is not.

steps.label: Constraint first, then approach
steps.note: Name the non-negotiable (revoke <=24h) BEFORE the pattern. A constraint that rules out no option is decoration — this one rules out manual removal.

steps.label: Selected approach
steps.note: SCIM push + a nightly RBAC matrix diff backstop. The backstop exists precisely because sync silently fails.

steps.label: Rejected approach + why
steps.note: Manual removal is rejected not because it is lazy but because it leaves no event trail — it is unprovable under operational evidence. Recording the rejection is the expert move.

steps.label: SCIM provisioning event replay
steps.note: The hook REPLAYS the offboard: CRM fired, SCIM sent DELETE, ITSM returned 200 — yet the role survived. Observed state contradicts the happy path.

steps.label: RBAC matrix diff
steps.note: Baseline (design) vs observed (live). The '+' line is the departed contractor still holding incident_admin — the exact go-live failure, caught by evidence, not opinion.

steps.label: Failure + reviewer objection + response
steps.note: The invalidation condition: access looks acceptable in review but fails when you replay the deprovision. The response points at observed state, never at the CRM event alone.

crm-itsm-patterns.text: The senior tell in enterprise SaaS: they never trust that an event was SENT — they prove the STATE it should have produced. 'CRM emitted the offboard' is inference; 'the RBAC matrix no longer lists her' is evidence. Audit-trail completeness means the log answers who/what/when for every elevation, not that it merely exists. Deprovisioning, not provisioning, is where vendor-risk lives.

crm-itsm-patterns.question: A reviewer challenges: 'Show me the exact evidence that CRM/ITSM access is proven, not just designed.' Which response actually proves it?
options: The RBAC role definitions from the design document, matching the approved architecture.
A SCIM provisioning event replay plus an RBAC matrix diff (baseline vs observed) showing a departed user's role removed — or flagged if still present.
A statement that SSO, SCIM, and audit logging are all enabled in the platform settings.
A screenshot of the admin console showing the SSO integration is 'Connected'.
crm-itsm-patterns.explanation: Only option 2 shows OBSERVED state changing under a replayed failure — the deprovision event replayed and the live-vs-baseline diff. Options 1, 3, and 4 all prove intent or configuration ('designed', 'enabled', 'Connected'), which is exactly the gap where the departed contractor keeps her admin. Access correctness is a claim about running state, and only a replay + diff observes it.

crm-itsm-patterns.intro: Prove your packet holds — no vibes, operational evidence only:
items: Your constraint (e.g. revoke <=24h after CRM offboard) rules out at least one plausible option. If it rules out nothing, it is decoration — sharpen it.
The rejected approach is recorded with WHY it fails under operational evidence (no event trail, silent drift), not just 'we chose the other one'.
At least two inspection-hook outputs are attached and were actually run: pick two of OIDC metadata review, SAML assertion checklist, SCIM provisioning event replay, RBAC matrix diff.
The verification proves observed state, not a fired event: an RBAC matrix diff or a replay that could return 'FAIL', not a screenshot that can only say 'Connected'.
You wrote the invalidation condition — the specific result under which this decision would be wrong (access acceptable in review but broken when operational evidence changes).
A second reviewer can replay one failure from the packet and reach the same conclusion without you narrating.

change-control.doNotClaim: Do not claim change control is 'in place' because a change was approved. Approval is a signature, not proof. If the packet has no failure trigger and no replayable verification, you documented a decision — you did not control the change.

change-control.text: Friday 4 p.m.: an admin toggles one RBAC role in the SaaS console to 'unblock' a launch. Monday, finance analysts can read payroll, the SCIM sync silently deprovisioned six contractors, and the audit log has a gap no one can explain. Nobody controlled the change — they just made it.

Change control is the gate between 'we decided to change identity, approvals, or an integration' and 'we can prove it did exactly that and nothing else.' It is Section 4 of the enterprise SaaS governance packet you carry through this module — the release-risk discipline that keeps access correct, records in sync, and the audit trail complete.

change-control.prompt: An admin says: 'The change is low-risk — I tested it in the console and access looked right.' Before you approve — what is wrong with 'access looked right' as proof? Answer before reading on.
change-control.reveal: 'Looked right' is a screenshot of the happy path, not a control. It proves one identity saw one screen; it says nothing about the RBAC matrix DIFF (who else silently gained or lost access), the SCIM provisioning events the change fired downstream, or whether the audit log even recorded the edit. Change control asks a harder question: what changed that you did NOT intend, and can you prove it did not? A change that looks acceptable in review but fails when release risk shifts is the exact failure this lesson exists to catch.

# Change Control Decision Packet

## Context
- System: Enterprise SaaS (identity + approvals + integrations + audit)
- Change: grant role `billing_read` to Finance-Ops (12 users), by <date>
- Reversibility: two-way door (role revocable) BUT SCIM deprovision = one-way

## Constraint (non-negotiable)
- No daytime deprovisioning on the payroll integration path

## Selected approach
- Scoped role add via IdP group; SCIM pushes grants only, deprovision disabled for window

## Rejected approach
- Direct in-console role edit — no RBAC diff, bypasses approval, invisible to SCIM replay

## Expected failure
- Role inheritance leaks `payroll_read`; SCIM fires unintended deprovisions; audit gap

## Verification method (inspection hooks)
- RBAC matrix diff: before vs after (expect delta = 12 users, 0 others)
- SCIM provisioning event replay: expect 12 provisions, 0 deprovisions
- SAML assertion checklist: group->role claim maps only to billing_read
- Audit trail sample: every grant row has actor + timestamp + approver

## Reviewer objection + response
- Objection: "proven or just described?" -> attach RBAC diff + SCIM replay log
steps: Predict the access, workflow, or audit decision before executing.
Context + reversibility: Name the change AND its reversibility per layer. A role edit is a two-way door; a SCIM deprovision is one-way. Mixed reversibility sets how much proof you owe.
The constraint that actually rules out an option: 'No daytime deprovisioning on the payroll path' eliminates the direct-console edit below. A constraint that rules out nothing is decoration.
Selected approach: Push grants through the IdP group so SCIM and the audit log both SEE the change. The approach is chosen for its inspectability, not its speed.

Rejected approach — and why it fails: The in-console edit is faster and completely uncontrolled: no RBAC diff, bypasses approval, invisible to SCIM replay. Naming why it fails under release risk is the senior move.
Expected failure: Specific enough to recognize in an audit: role inheritance leaks payroll_read, unintended SCIM deprovisions, an audit gap. Names both over-grant and silent-loss.

Verification via at least two inspection hooks: RBAC matrix diff + SCIM event replay are the two load-bearing hooks. Each must be able to return 'no' — a diff that can only say 'looks fine' is theater.
Change one owner, role, lifecycle, retry, mapping, or evidence assumption and identify the required repair.

A second reviewer can point to the exact evidence and replay the failure without you narrating.

storyboard.say: Every change starts as an explicit request, not a hunch — someone names the intended change and submits it to the gate.
The approval gate is the checkpoint: nothing reaches identity or the app until an approved change is authorized to pass.
Only approved, the IdP provisions the role into the SaaS app — SAML and SCIM carry the change into production identity.
The SaaS app records the event to the audit log, so every landed change leaves a complete, replayable trace.
The audit log feeds the no-drift proof: RBAC matrix diff, SCIM event replay, and audit-trail completeness all get checked.
The proof reports back to the gate — an approved change without a replayable no-drift proof is uncontrolled, so the gate needs it.
The Friday failure is the bypass: editing the console directly skips the gate — that path must be blocked or drift goes unproven.

change-control.text: The senior tell in enterprise SaaS: they prove what did NOT change, not just what did. Anyone can screenshot the intended grant. A change controller attaches the RBAC matrix diff whose delta is exactly the intended set — because the dangerous failures (role bleed, silent SCIM deprovision, an audit gap) all live in the rows you did not mean to touch. Standards like SOX and SOC 2 change management ask the same question: separation of duties, approval, and an inspectable trail — not 'trust me, it worked.'

change-control.question: A reviewer challenges: 'Show me this change was controlled, not just approved.' Which single piece of evidence best answers that?
options: A screenshot of the admin console showing the new role assigned to the Finance-Ops team.
An RBAC matrix diff (before vs after) whose delta equals exactly the intended users, plus a SCIM event replay showing only the intended provisions and zero unintended deprovisions.
The Slack message where the manager wrote 'approved, go ahead.'
A note in the ticket saying the change was tested and access looked correct.
change-control.explanation: Change control proves the ACTUAL diff equals the INTENDED diff and nothing else moved. Only the RBAC matrix diff plus SCIM replay can return 'no' — they catch role bleed and silent deprovisioning in the rows you did not touch. A screenshot (1) shows one happy path; an approval (3) is a signature, not proof; 'looked correct' (4) is a vibe. The failures live in what you did not check.

change-control.intro: Prove your change was controlled — no vibes:
items: Read your intended change aloud as a diff ("+12 users to role X, 0 others"). If you can only describe it in prose, you cannot prove drift — restate it as a delta.
Run the RBAC matrix diff before vs after. Confirm the delta equals exactly the intended set. Any extra granted or revoked identity is uncontrolled drift — investigate before unlock.
Replay the SCIM provisioning events. Confirm the count and direction match intent (provisions vs deprovisions). A silent deprovision on a one-way path is the highest-severity finding.
Check the constraint actually ruled out an option: name the approach your constraint eliminated (e.g. the direct-console edit). If none, the constraint is decoration.
Sample the audit trail for the change: every affected grant has an actor, a timestamp, and an approver. A gap means the change is invisible to a future auditor — the trail is incomplete.
Confirm change_control_risk_register.md lists the top three residual risks the decision did NOT resolve — so the packet does not hide unresolved release risk.

api-and-webhook-integration.text: An offboarded contractor still shows Active in three downstream systems a week after HR pressed Deactivate — the SCIM deprovision fired, but one webhook 401'd on a rotated secret and nobody was listening for the failure. The audit finds a ghost account with live access, and no one can say who owned the sync.

This is lesson 1 of Integrations, Data & Audit: the moment your SaaS estate stops being a set of apps and becomes a system where identity, roles, and records must stay in agreement across boundaries. API and webhook integration is where boundary and ownership are decided — or silently lost.

api-and-webhook-integration.prompt: You wire two SaaS apps together. Which is safer to build your sync on: the source app POSTs you a webhook the moment a user changes, or you poll its API on a schedule? Decide before reading.
api-and-webhook-integration.reveal: Trick question — neither alone is safe, and 'webhook' is the seductive wrong answer. Webhooks are fire-and-forget: the sender POSTs once, and if you 401, time out, or your endpoint is down, that event is gone and your systems now disagree with no error anywhere. The gold pattern is webhook for latency PLUS a reconciling poll (or SCIM replay) as the source of truth that catches every event the webhook dropped. A webhook is a notification, never a ledger.

storyboard.say: It starts with a lifecycle event: HR presses Deactivate, telling the Identity Provider, our single source of truth for identity.
The IdP provisions that change outward through the SCIM Bridge, the API path that keeps downstream apps in agreement.
SCIM sets the role in the Downstream SaaS, and records proof of the deprovision to the Audit Log.
To notify the world of the change fast, the SaaS emits an event to the Webhook Receiver, our low-latency path.
Here is the failure: on a rotated secret the webhook 401s and drops, so nobody hears it and the SaaS keeps a stale Active role.
The Reconciler is the safety net: fed the true state, it diffs the IdP against the SaaS and heals the drift the webhook lost.
Reconciliation records its proof to the Audit Log, so the ghost account cannot hide and every sync failure is replayable.
The invariant: even if a webhook is silently dropped, reconciliation still converges, so identity and roles cannot drift out of agreement.

data-sync-contract.prompt: Two systems both write the user's `department` field — HR's HRIS and the SaaS app's admin console. Both are 'live' and 'authoritative'. What actually happens over time? Answer before reading on.
data-sync-contract.reveal: They diverge, silently. With no declared system of record, the last writer wins per sync, so `department` flips back and forth depending on which job ran most recently — a race condition across systems. RBAC keyed on `department` then grants and revokes access on a coin flip, and the audit log shows a value that was never stably true. The fix is not 'sync more often'; it is deciding, in writing, that exactly one system owns each field and the other is read-only for it.

data-sync-contract.title: The identity sync path — where records drift
data-sync-contract.subtitle: HRIS is system of record for lifecycle + department; the IdP provisions via SCIM into the SaaS app; RBAC and the audit log read downstream. The suspect edge is the SCIM deprovision hop. Billing and the CRM are deliberately out of scope.

nodes.label: Conflict rule
nodes.description: HRIS wins on status; app wins on app-local prefs

storyboard.say: HR is the system of record: when a contractor is terminated, the HRIS fires a lifecycle event into the identity provider.
The IdP is supposed to push that change into the SaaS app over SCIM, provisioning on hire and deprovisioning on exit.
This SCIM deprovision hop is the suspect edge. It lags, so the SaaS app keeps the contractor marked active for weeks.
Worse, no contract declared a single writer, so the conflict rule never resolves who owns the status field when systems disagree.
Downstream, RBAC reads department to grant roles, so the stale active status keeps the offboarded user's access live.
Both the SaaS app and HRIS emit change events to the audit log, which is how the gap gets found after the fact.
The fix: one writer per field, a declared sync cadence, and a reconciliation check that makes drift observable instead of silent.
